source.title_on_document: Story Forge: A Card-Based Framework for AI-Assisted Interactive Storytelling

supplement.where: Appendix A. Narrative Output Cases, pp. 31-32 of this PDF, cited in Section 4.5 (p. 21). No separate supplementary file or online appendix is referenced. The Data Availability Statement (p. 31) says the data are on University of Plymouth's OneDrive, with no link.
supplement.holds: Two screenshots of AI-generated story steps from typical card combinations. No statistics: every number recorded in this form is in the main text.

paper_design_summary: Thirty university students (30 analyzed, no exclusions reported) were randomly divided between a control group that wrote interactive branching stories with Squibler's web-based AI Story Writer and an experimental group that used Story Forge, the authors' card-based interface that turns selected story cards into prompts for the Doubao 3.5 language model. Each arm ran as three sessions of five participants, 35 minutes each. Outcomes are metrics from interaction records and path analyses (writing time, decisions, path branches, choice coverage, repeat visits, new-path discovery), a causal relationship strength score whose computation the paper does not describe, and self-reported SUS, Creativity Support Index, and User Participation Index scores. No rater or computed score of the creativity or diversity of the stories is reported.

studies.label: Story Forge vs AI Story Writer, interactive story writing (30 students)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Writing tool: Story Forge, the authors' card-based interface on the Doubao 3.5 LLM (experimental), or Squibler's web-based AI Story Writer (control)
assignment.quote: Participants were randomly divided into a control group and an experimental group.

arms.name: Story Forge (experimental)
arms.description: Card-based adaptive story interface: users drag character, event/plot, emotion, and optional scene cards into story-stage slots, and the Doubao LLM (Version 3.5, ByteDance) generates branching story text and choices from the card combination (Unity front end, Node.js back end). Three sessions of five, 35 min each, after a 10 min training session.

arms.name: AI Story Writer (control)
arms.description: Squibler's web-based AI Story Generator (genre menu, creativity slider, story-plot prompt box), with a predetermined story theme and creation duration. Three sessions of five, 35 min each, after a 10 min training session.

participants.exclusions: None reported. No results table prints an n. The 30 analyzed rests on 30 enrolled (p. 19), 30 recruited (p. 20), 30 story drafts at the end, 15 per arm (p. 21), and 'a sample of 30 participants' (p. 29). Per-arm 15 follows from three groups of five per arm (pp. 19-20) and the 15 drafts per arm (p. 21).
participants.who: University students (15 male, 15 female) with expertise in AI tools and story creation (M = 2.53, SD = 0.95); none had prior exposure to the narrative writing system. Section 5.6 (p. 29) instead describes 'predominantly university students' with '70% students' and mean writing experience of 15.4 years, which conflicts with pp. 19-20.
participants.country: not_stated (authors at the University of Plymouth, UK; funding from the Chinese Government Scholarship)
participants.quote: We enrolled 30 university students (15 males, 15 females) with expertise in AI tools and story creation (M = 2.53, SD = 0.95) into a study.
participants.locator: p. 19, Section 4.3; p. 20, Section 4.3 (power analysis, 30 recruited; three control and three experimental groups); p. 21, Section 4.5 (30 story drafts, 15 per arm); p. 29, Section 5.6

ai_tool.name_model: Treatment: Story Forge on the Doubao AI LLM (Version 3.5, ByteDance), Unity front end and Node.js back end. Control: Squibler AI Story Writer (web tool, 'version Squibler 2025'; underlying model not stated).
ai_tool.how_used: In Story Forge, users select and arrange story-element cards (character, event, emotion, scene) in slots; the system converts the combination into a structured prompt and the LLM generates branching story text and choices. In the control, users enter a story-plot prompt with genre and creativity settings and the tool generates the story. Both arms had generative AI throughout the session.

task.description: Interactive branching story creation: story creation, plot expansion, and branching plot development on a predetermined story theme.
task.duration: 35 min session after a 10 min training session; individual interviews averaged 25 min afterwards (pp. 20-21)

outcomes.question: none

outcomes.name: Causal relationship strength (0-1)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: 'Causal Relationship Reasonableness Diagram (Node Connection Strength)', from 'Quantitative Analysis of Logical Relationship Diagram' (Table 4, p. 19). The paper never says which diagram is analyzed or how strength is computed. The text reads the result as users' comprehension of narrative causal links (p. 22) and 'perceived causal relationship strength' (p. 25), and p. 21 lists 'causal event triggers' among logged user data, while Section 5.4.4 (p. 28) discusses the stories' causal chains and text coherence. The authors also say the evaluation lacks 'third-party objective assessment of the quality of the content that is produced' (p. 29), and they plan blind expert ratings of 'logical coherence' for future work (p. 30). scored_on_output = false is provisional (see reconciliation). If the score were computed on the stories, it would measure causal coherence, not creativity or diversity. Whether coherence counts as quality under usefulness is a codebook question for Review 1 (final.open_items). One of the 'two primary metrics' in the FDR analysis (p. 25).

eligibility.reason: Criterion 1 met: individuals were randomly divided between two generative-AI story tools, Story Forge and Squibler's AI Story Writer (p. 19, Section 4.3; abstract, p. 1), an ai_design contrast. Criterion 2 not met: 30 people were enrolled and randomized, and the form counts all 30 as analyzed because no exclusions are reported (pp. 19-21, 29). That is well below 50, and the paper gives no other count of people. Criterion 3 not met: no outcome scores the creativity, novelty, or cross-person diversity of the stories. The outcomes are interaction-record and path metrics and self-reported SUS, CSI, and UPI, and the authors say the evaluation lacks 'third-party objective assessment of the quality of the content that is produced' (p. 29). The one open point is causal relationship strength. The paper does not say how it is computed and reads it as users' comprehension of causal links (p. 22). If it scores each story's causal coherence, Review 1 decides whether coherence counts as quality under usefulness (final.open_items). The two trained raters on p. 21 rated collaboration levels, and no results from them are reported. Output metrics listed on p. 21 (word count, diversity of story elements) are also not reported. Core is no under any answer, because criterion 2 fails.

one_line_finding: With 30 students randomly split between two AI story tools, Story Forge users had higher choice coverage (70.4 vs 52.9 percent, t = 5.58, p = 0.012, d = 1.21) and similar causal relationship strength (0.76 vs 0.74, p = 0.531), the paper's two primary metrics (p. 22, Table 7; pp. 24-25), and higher self-reported Creativity Support Index scores (3.9 vs 3.5, d = 0.53, FDR-corrected p = 0.061; p. 24, Table 9; p. 25), but the paper reports no creativity or diversity rating of the stories.
open_questions: Printed test statistics are internally inconsistent. Every printed d fits the printed means and SDs (Section 5.2, pp. 24-25). But with 15 per arm, those means and SDs give t of about 1.3 for dwell time and 3.3 for choice coverage, against the printed 2.04 and 5.58 (Tables 6-7, p. 22), and every printed t fits about 36 to 43 per arm. The printed p values imply about 2.5 to 105 degrees of freedom across rows, none near 28 (for example t = 5.41 with p = 0.015, Table 6, p. 22). The paper does not say what the tests counted, so the test statistics may be unreliable.

Per-arm analyzed n is never printed. Fifteen per arm is implied by three groups of five per arm (pp. 19-20) and 15 story drafts per arm (p. 21), but '95% of the experimental group participants' (p. 27) is not a whole number of 15 people. The printed t values fit about 40 per arm (open question 1).

Sample description conflicts: '30 university students' (p. 19) and 'all participants are university students' (p. 20) versus 'predominantly university students' with '70% students' and mean writing experience of 15.4 years (p. 29).

Scale ranges conflict: CSI 7-point, UPI 6-point, and SUS 5-point with a 0-100 total (p. 18), but all three are 1-5 in Table 4 (p. 19) and 1-7 on p. 21. The printed means (3.5 to 4.0, Table 9) are not on a 0-100 SUS total, and the Figure 12 boxplots show an SUS value near 6 and a UPI value above 5 (p. 24), above a 1-5 range.

Section 4.3 (pp. 19-20) says the same 30 students 'were selected for the pilot study to validate the fundamental features of the system', and the abstract mentions 'two tests'. Whether the pilot and the comparative experiment are the same sessions is unclear.
Sessions ran in groups of five (three per arm, p. 20), and the paper reports independent-sample t-tests with no adjustment for session (p. 1, Abstract; Tables 6-9).

The paper does not say which diagram yields causal relationship strength or how node connection strength is computed (Table 4, p. 19), so whether that outcome scores the stories is unclear. If it does score the stories, it scores their causal coherence, and Review 1 decides whether coherence counts as quality under usefulness.

Two trained raters evaluated 'collaboration levels' (p. 21), but no rater results are reported. Output metrics listed on p. 21 (word count, diversity of story elements, emotional tags) are not reported either.

Section 4.4 (p. 20) calls Doubao 'the sole control variable', yet the control arm used Squibler's AI Story Writer, whose model is not stated. Whether the arms differ in the underlying model is unclear.

Boxplots show values outside the stated ranges: story writing time up to about 41 min, although each session lasted 35 min (Figure 9, p. 22; p. 20), and choice coverage above 100 percent (a control outlier near 106) and causal relationship strength above 1 on its 0-1 axis (Figure 10, p. 23).
notes: All ten quantitative outcomes in Tables 6-9 are listed with question 'none' to document why criterion 3 fails. None scores the creativity or diversity of the written stories. Exploration path complexity and causal relationship strength come from analyses of path structure and of a logical relationship diagram (Table 4), but the paper reads them as exploration behavior and users' comprehension of causal links, not as creativity. Qualitative interview outcomes (Table 5, Section 5.3) are not listed. Section 3.6 (pp. 15-17) compares Story Forge with GPT-4o and NovelAI on one example narrative, with no participants and no scored outcome. Section 5.6 (p. 29) says the risk of generative-AI homogenization (Doshi and Hauser 2024) 'was not thoroughly explored in this study'. Finalizer, 2026-10-05: no challenge file exists for c140 (forms/challenges/c140.*.json matches nothing), because the finish-18 run ran challenges only for c075, c109, and c126 (RESUME.md). So final.challenge_resolution is empty and its three counts are zero. The finalizer instead read the whole markdown and checked PDF pp. 1-8 and 17-34 on the page image. Every number in Tables 6-9 and Section 5.2, every quote, and every locator in the form match the PDF. Edits: source.version now gives the citation as p. 1 prints it ('Electronics 2025, 14, 2955'), because the issue number appears only inside the DOI. paper_design_summary now says 'analyzed' and no longer lists causal relationship strength among the interaction-log metrics. S1-O2 measure_detail adds the authors' statements on pp. 29-30 and the codebook question on coherence. eligibility.reason now treats each criterion in turn. Open questions 1, 2, 4, 6, and 7 are extended, and open question 10 is new. Open question 1 rests on a consistency check, not on recorded statistics: every printed d fits the printed means and SDs, but the printed t values fit about 36 to 43 per arm, and the printed p values imply about 2.5 to 105 degrees of freedom. The figure values in open questions 4 and 10 were read from high-resolution renders of the boxplots and are approximate.

reconciliation.notes: Both raw forms parse. The markdown is complete (920 lines) and matches the PDF. The whole markdown was read, and PDF pp. 1, 7, 13-14, and 17-34 were checked page by page, including every number in Tables 6-9 and Section 5.2. Wording-only differences (study label, arm descriptions, design summaries, participant and company-involvement locators, the choice of participant quote, open questions, notes) were merged without entries. The one unresolved item, whether causal relationship strength is scored on the stories, does not change eligibility: the paper fails criteria 2 and 3 either way.

open_items.item: Printed test statistics that do not fit the printed means and SDs at 15 per arm (open question 1). Every printed d fits the means and SDs, but every printed t fits about 36 to 43 per arm, and the printed p values imply about 2.5 to 105 degrees of freedom across rows (Tables 6-9, pp. 22-24; Section 5.2, pp. 24-25). Criterion 2 counts people, and the paper gives 30 people at every mention (pp. 19, 20, 21, 29), so more test rows would not mean more people. The statistics matter for extraction, and this paper stays out of the dataset. The Data Availability Statement names the University of Plymouth's OneDrive with no link (p. 31).

Per-arm analyzed n (open question 2). Fifteen per arm follows from three sessions of five per arm (pp. 19-20) and 15 drafts per arm (p. 21), but '95% of the experimental group participants' (p. 27) is not a whole number of 15 people. The total is 30 people under any split, below 50, so criterion 2 does not depend on it.

Sample description (open question 3): 'all participants are university students' (p. 20) against '70% students' and mean writing experience of 15.4 years (p. 29). It changes the population description, not the count of 30 people or any criterion.

Scale ranges of SUS, CSI, and UPI (open question 4): 5-, 7-, and 6-point on p. 18, 1-5 in Table 4 (p. 19), and 1-7 on p. 21, with Figure 12 values above 5 (p. 24). All three are self-reports, which cannot meet criterion 3 under any scale.

Pilot study versus comparative experiment (open question 5): the same 30 students were 'selected for the pilot study' (p. 19), and the abstract mentions 'two tests' (p. 1). No other sample is described, so no study in the paper has more than 30 people.

Session clustering (open question 6): sessions ran in groups of five, three per arm (p. 20), and the reported independent-sample t-tests make no adjustment for session. This bears on standard errors (codebook Section 10), not on any criterion.

Whether causal relationship strength (S1-O2) is computed on each participant's story (open question 7 and the one unresolved reconciliation difference). Table 4 names a 'Quantitative Analysis of Logical Relationship Diagram' but no procedure (p. 19). The text reads the result as users' comprehension (p. 22) and 'perceived' strength (p. 25), and the authors plan expert ratings of 'logical coherence' only for future work (p. 30). If the score is computed on the stories, Review 1 decides whether causal coherence counts as quality under usefulness, which would bear on criterion 3, as with the quality composite in c059. Core stays no under any answer, because only 30 people took part.

Unreported rater and output measures (open question 8). Two trained raters evaluated 'collaboration levels' (p. 21), which is not a score of the stories' creativity. Word count and 'diversity of story elements' are described only as metrics that 'can be analyzed' (p. 21), and no values appear, so no outcome of this kind can be coded. Core stays no because only 30 people took part.

Underlying model of the control tool (open question 9): Section 4.4 calls Doubao 'the sole control variable' (p. 20), but the control arm used Squibler's AI Story Writer, whose model is not stated (p. 6). Both arms used generative AI, so criterion 1 is met and the contrast is ai_design under any answer.

Plotted values outside the stated ranges (open question 10): story writing time up to about 41 min in 35-min sessions (Figure 9, p. 22), and choice coverage above 100 percent and causal relationship strength above 1 (Figure 10, p. 23). Like open question 1, this bears on the reliability of the statistics, not on eligibility.
